submission.natural_language_explanation: Retrospective token-type (unigram) detector: it fires on whichever word-piece is at the current position when that piece belongs to a scattered descriptive-appearance lexicon - colour/appearance words (colour, coloured, colourful, visual, appearance, look, view, symbol, image, sketch, icon, display, layout, panel, detail), ornament/ceremony words (ceremony, ribbon, icing, wrapping, curtain, decoration, styled, fancy, festive) and words for being noticeably or unusually visible (conspicuous, obscure, exotic, prominently, spotlight, unusual, strangely, quirky) - and sits at the GELU floor for basic concrete nouns, function words and plain technical identifiers in the same sentence frames (garden, window, river, mountain, flower, door, bottle, basket, shoulder, string, function, integer all near 0.00). It reads the word-piece and not the sentence, so a BPE fragment of a trigger word fires as hard as the whole word and often much harder ('pper' 1.23 inside 'Wrapper' while the single token ' wrapper' scores 0.03; 'oration' 1.24 in 'decoration'; 'View' 1.29 in 'tableView'; 'Details' and 'Topics' inside camelCase identifiers), which is why code and markup dominate its scan hits, and the same token scores within 0.1 of itself across five unrelated carrier sentences.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Last spring I joined a birdwatching group that met before sunrise at the edge of the county park. The leader, a retired teacher named Marta, handed out laminated checklists and warned us to keep our voices low. For the first hour we saw nothing but sparrows and a single crow on a fence post. The path curved along a drainage ditch, past a stone wall and a stand of dead oaks, and the air smelled of wet leaves. Marta stopped every few minutes to identify a call or to point out a nest high in the branches. Nobody in the group had much experience, and the conversation stayed on ordinary things: the cold, the forecast, the price of petrol, a recent storm that had knocked down two trees near the entrance. Around seven o'clock, near the far pond, someone pointed at a shape moving through the reeds. It was a bittern, and it stood out prominently against the pale water, its streaked plumage oddly conspicuous beside the smooth green stems. Marta whispered that the species had not been recorded here for eleven years. We watched it for perhaps twenty minutes while the light slowly changed from grey to gold. Afterwards the group drifted back toward the parking lot, trading guesses about why the bird had come. Someone said the drought farther south had pushed it north; another blamed the new ditch. Nobody really knew. I wrote the sighting in my notebook, drew a rough outline of the bird, and promised to send the record to the county naturalist. On the drive home I kept thinking about how a single quiet animal could turn an ordinary morning into something worth remembering.

At home I made tea and searched the species in an old field guide that had belonged to my grandfather. The entry described its habitat carefully, though the book was printed long before the pond was dug. I marked the page with a scrap of paper so I could find it again, then sat by the kitchen door and listened to the rain start on the roof. It seemed odd that a bird could travel so far and arrive without anyone seeing it until someone with binoculars happened to glance at the right patch of reeds at the right moment. Perhaps that is how most discoveries happen, quietly and by accident, on an ordinary morning when no one expects anything at all.
